steps: Unpack & inspect

Check permits with local building officials and notify your insurer. Remove the cardboard from inside the smoke outlet before touching the rear baffle, inspect for damage, then unscrew the firebox from its pallet brackets and lift it free.

• Contents: firebox with firebricks, draw-down flue collar adaptor with pins, stove hardware bag, Fireplace Conversion Notice Plate, catalyst temperature probe and reader, blower power cord, AC power receptacle lead, two leg levelers. The surround kit is packed separately.
  • Removing the rear baffle before the cardboard packing will damage the baffle.
  • Avoid tipping the insert in transport; baffles and catalyst can be damaged. Lighten it by removing the door (keep the door washer) and firebricks.
  • Report dents, cracked glass or broken bricks to the dealer.
Do not lift the firebox from the rear opening. Doing so may damage the secondary air assembly (p. 5).
Qualify the fireplace

Solid masonry only, never a factory-built fireplace. Clean and inspect to NFPA 211 (a Level II inspection) before installing, repair cracks or broken bricks and flue tiles, and seal hearth-extension gaps with medium-duty refractory mortar.
Lay out hearth protection

UL listed Type II hearth board or equivalent mortared masonry (R-value 1.1): 16" (U.S.) / 20" (Canada) forward of the door opening and 18 1/2" each side of centerline. Hold the side-trim, top-trim and mantel clearances.
Prepare the chimney

Remove the damper and linkage or wire the plate open; wire-brush the firebox and smoke shelf. If the fireplace was modified, anchor Fireplace Conversion Notice Plate PN 220508 to the rear wall; fit a damper sealing plate if appropriate.
Route the blower power cord

Pick a side, never across the front. Fit the AC power receptacle lead in that side's inlet, plug the harness into the blower connector between the two blowers, and don't plug into the wall until the install is complete.

1. Remove the #8 x 5/8" phillips screw at the inlet, engage the receptacle bracket with the tab in the opening, and reinstall the screw from the inside.
  2. Route the AC wire harness through the hole in the Inner Shroud and around the front of the blower. Loosen the Control Switchplate wing nut to swing the switch assembly out for access to the connector.
  3. After connecting, relocate the harness behind the blower and resecure the switchplate.

Optional Blower Flex Conduit Kit 158002 (p. 15): route the conduit through the masonry to 110vac at a junction box, or under the firebox to an ash dump using the riser frame; seal seams and holes against air infiltration; ground the blowers per local code or ANSI/NFPA 70 / CSA C22.1; cap the unused receptacle opening and test the blowers before final positioning.
Install the catalyst probe

Remove the probe access door (top right) and the bolt inside; anti-seize the probe threads, feed it through the right-side slot, hand-start it and tighten carefully with a 10mm wrench. Do not over-tighten.

1. Remove the access door screw with a 1/4" nut driver; lift off the Probe Access Door.
  2. Remove the bolt inside the probe access area with a 10mm wrench.
  3. Apply anti-seize compound to the probe threads and feed the threaded end through the slot on the right side.
  4. Hand-start it in the threaded hole, then tighten carefully with a 10mm wrench.
  5. Refit the access door. Route the probe wire down the side to the front grate or through the right side.
Fit the draw-down adaptor

Lift out the rear baffle and rear air tube for flue access. Fasten the liner in the adaptor with three sheet metal screws, set the insert, pull the adaptor into the flue collar and lock it with the retainer and cotter pins; refit tube and baffle.

1. Open the door; lift the rear baffle and slide it back to rest on the rear manifold member.
  2. Rotate the rear air tube retainer clip (left side) counter clockwise to horizontal and pull it toward the front.
  3. Slide the rear tube right, pull its left side forward while moving it left, and remove it.
  4. Lift the rear refractory baffle off the manifold, shift it left and forward, and remove it.
  5. Push the flex liner as far as it will go into the adaptor's non-crimped end (or the liner maker's adaptor), with the retainer pin parallel to the fireplace front; drill through the three pilot holes and fit three sheet metal screws.
  6. Set the insert in its final position, reach up and pull the adaptor into the flue collar, insert the retainer pin through the adaptor ears and lock it with the cotter pin.
  7. Reverse the steps to reinstall the baffles and tubes.
The combustor does not need to come out for flue access. If it is removed after the first firing, a new gasket kit (158406) must be ordered.
Level the firebox

If the hearth is uneven, tilt the firebox with a helper and thread the two leveler bolts into the tapped floor holes about 6" from the rear; adjust for lateral level and vertical plumb so the surround aligns.
Attach the surround

Cast iron: assemble breastplates, legs and plinth face-down, fit the bottom trim, hang the surround on the side brackets, adjust the set screw for bowing and push it flush. Steel: pull the blower control bracket forward, remove the door, seat the tabs in the large side slots.
Break-in fires

Three or four progressively hotter fires with the air fully open, cooling completely between them; the first is kindling and a couple of 1 -2 inch logs. Chimney draft should be in the .05 - 1.0 w.c. range.

panels.title: Over-firing
items: Insert or chimney connector glows → over-firing; close the air control immediately
Door left partly open → over-firing; gas and flame can be drawn out of the stove
Signs: any part glowing red, warped plates, rust-colored cast iron, paint turned dusty white, bubbling or cracked enamel

panels.title: Combustor performance lagging
items: Monitor falls below 500°F at medium to medium-low air after two or three hours of hot burning → clean or replace the combustor (repeat the test 2-3 times)
Lost heating efficiency, more creosote and emissions → combustor not functioning
Junk mail or lots of newsprint used to start fires → faster fly-ash build-up on the combustor
Catalyst cell collapse or degraded insulation panels → replace the damaged parts

panels.title: Smoke, draft & creosote
items: Exhaust fan or clothes dryer lowering room pressure → flow reversal through the stove and chimney
Burning at the lowest air settings → incomplete combustion, weak draft, cool flue, rapid creosote
Wood above 12 - 20% moisture → inefficient burn, creosote in the cool flue
Exterior chimney → more prone to creosote than an interior flue

panels.title: Blowers not running
items: Speed control off → the snapstat (Automatic) won't start the blowers
Fire not yet established → the snapstat starts them after the fire has burned for a time
Ash piled at the center front of the firebox → automatic blower may not work properly

start.title: Starting a fire
start.html:
Build every fire directly on the bottom grate. Don't raise it up in any way, and never use gasoline, kerosene, lighter fluid or similar liquids to start it.

Traditional way

  1. Push the air lever all the way to the right (fully open).
  2. Lay several sheets of crumpled newspaper on the grate. Add small, dry kindling about 1" across, then two or three logs about 3" to 5" across on top.
  3. Light it and close the door. Build the fire slowly with larger and larger logs.
  4. Once it's well established, set the air lever for the heat and burn time you want.

Top-down way

Many people like this better. With the lever fully open, lay two short 1/4-split logs on the floor about 6 inches apart, running front to back. Lay kindling across them and one or two smaller logs on top. Tuck newspaper between the bottom logs, under the kindling, light it and close the door. Keep the air fully open until the fire is well established.

New insert? Break it in first with three or four fires, each a bit hotter than the last, letting it cool completely in between. Keep the first one to kindling and a couple of 1 -2 inch logs, with the air fully open. Some odor and smoke in the first few fires is normal as residues burn off and the paint cures. Open a nearby window.

air.title: Setting the air control
air.html:
A single lever, in the slot at the upper right of the insert's front, sets how much air feeds the fire. All the way right is fully open.

  • Starting or reviving a fire: push it all the way right.
  • Turning it down: keep it fully open until the combustor monitor reads 500°F, hold that for 15-20 minutes, then move it to a medium-low to medium-high setting.
  • More air gives a hotter fire that burns wood faster. Less air gives less heat and a slower burn.

Burn rates

Low5/32" open · blower Low / On at 30 min.
Medium low3/16"-5/16" open · blower Low / On at 30 min.
Medium high5/16"-1/2" open · blower Low / On at 30 min.
HighMax. open · blower High / On

A more open setting also keeps the glass cleaner, because the same air washes over it. Try not to burn at the very lowest settings: the longer burn comes with a cooler chimney and fast creosote build-up.

Do not over-fire. Glowing means over-firing. If the insert or chimney connector glows, close the air control right away.

reload.title: Adding wood
reload.html:
Reload while there's still a bed of hot embers:

  1. Put on stove gloves.
  2. Push the air lever all the way right (fully open).
  3. Wait a few seconds before you open the door. The extra air clears unburned gases out of the firebox first.
  4. Open the door slowly. Spread the hot embers evenly with a poker or stove tool, and clear ash away from the center front of the firebox so the automatic blower works properly.
  5. Load the wood, usually smaller logs first, and keep it behind the andirons.
  6. Close the door and latch it.
  7. Wait 5 – 10 minutes for the fire to pick back up, then set the air lever. With a thick bed of live coals, you may be able to set it right away.
Keep logs at least one inch off the glass, and never use the door to push wood in.
Run the insert only with the door fully closed. A door left partly open can over-fire it and draw flame and smoke out of the stove.

monitor.title: Reading the combustor monitor
monitor.html:
Your insert has a catalytic combustor above the fire. The combustor monitor reads the temperature right behind it, so you can see how efficiently the fire is burning.

Turn the air down after500°F, held 15-20 minutes
Most efficient500°F to 800°F
Can reach1400°F to 1500°F

The probe wire comes out on the right side. Plug it into the monitor with the positive and negative prongs lined up with the markings.

Keep the combustor working

  • Look at it at least three times a heating season: open the door and look up at it with a flashlight.
  • Sweep loose fly ash off its cells with a soft brush. The cells are fragile.
  • Don't remove it to clean it. Taking it out means fitting a new insulation wrap.
  • Starting fires with junk mail or lots of newspaper clogs it with fly ash faster.
If the monitor won't stay at 500°F or higher on medium to medium-low air after a good hot fire, the combustor may need cleaning or replacing. Ask your Jøtul dealer.
It's against federal regulations to run this insert with the catalytic element removed or deactivated.

wood.title: What wood to burn
wood.html:
Burn natural, untreated wood only. Air-dried, seasoned hardwood burns more efficiently and more cleanly than softwood or green wood.

  • Seasoning: wood air-dried for 6 to 14 months gives the cleanest, most efficient heat. Wood seasoned more than 2 years burns too fast.
  • Moisture: aim for 12 - 20%. A moisture meter is the surest check. Seasoned logs show cracks (check marks) on the ends and feel lighter.
  • Wet wood spends its heat driving out water and leaves creosote in the chimney, which raises the risk of a chimney fire.

Never burn

Coal, garbage, synthetic logs, anything with rubber or plastic, petroleum products, asphalt products, paints, paint thinners or solvents, asbestos, construction or demolition debris, railroad ties or pressure-treated wood, manure or animal remains, yard waste, salt-water driftwood, unseasoned wood, colored paper, junk mail, cardboard, plywood or particle board. Fire starters made from paper, cardboard, sawdust or wax are fine for lighting.

These can give off toxic fumes, including carbon monoxide, and can damage the catalytic combustor and void your warranty. Never use gasoline, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or freshen up a fire.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
Now and then you'll need to clean carbon and fly ash off the glass. Left on too long, deposits can etch the glass and make it cloudy. Creosote deposits should burn off in the next hot fire.

  1. Wait until the glass is completely cool.
  2. Use only a cleaner made for this job. Never use anything abrasive: it damages the glass and leaves a frosted surface. Crumpled newspaper works especially well.
  3. Rinse and dry the glass completely before you light a fire.

Burning with the air control more open helps the glass stay clean.

Cracked or broken glass? Don't use the insert until it's replaced. Get the replacement glass made for the C 550 V2 from your Jøtul dealer, with no substitutes. Open and close the door slowly, never slam it, and don't strike the glass.

chimney.title: Ashes and chimney care
chimney.html:
Ashes

  • Wear stove gloves. Put ashes in a metal container with a tight-fitting lid.
  • Set the closed container on a noncombustible floor or on the ground, well away from anything that can burn. If you bury or scatter the ashes, keep them in the closed container until all the cinders have cooled.
  • Leave a thin layer of ash on the firebox floor. Never use a household vacuum on ashes.

Creosote and your chimney

A slow, low-temperature fire sends tar and other vapors up the chimney, where they condense as creosote. Creosote is highly flammable: it's the fuel of chimney fires.

  • Have the chimney and connector cleaned and inspected at the start of each heating season, and inspect them every other month while you're using the insert.
  • Have the chimney cleaned whenever creosote builds up to 1/4" or more. Your dealer can refer you to a professional chimney sweep.
  • Dry wood and avoiding the lowest air settings keep creosote down. An exterior chimney collects more creosote than one inside the house.

While you're at it, check the firebox inside and out with a utility light for cracks or leaks.

blower.title: Using the blowers
blower.html:
Two blowers move heat from around the firebox out into the room.

  • Controls: the speed knob can be reached from the front. The switch is behind the cast-iron lower grille (lift it off) or the steel surround (remove it).
  • Automatic: a heat sensor turns the blowers on once the fire has burned for a while, and off again as it dies down. It only works with the speed control on.
  • Manual: the blowers run whatever the temperature.
  • Off: for when you don't need them.

For best results, don't switch them on until the fire is well established.

Keep them clean

Unplug the blower power cord first. Remove the front grille (cast surround) or the whole steel surround, then vacuum the blower housing, its compartment and the area under the firebox with a soft brush attachment. Do it regularly, especially if you have pets.

The cord has a three-prong grounding plug. Plug it straight into a grounded three-prong outlet, never cut off the grounding prong, and use only the cord supplied.

safety.title: Safety around the insert
safety.html:
• The insert gets extremely hot. Keep children, clothing and furniture away: touching it will burn skin. Wear stove gloves when you tend the fire.
  • Keep anything that can burn at least 36" from the front, including drapes and doors that could swing into that space.
  • Never run it with cracked or broken glass, or with the door partly open.
  • Burn solid wood only. Don't use chemicals or fluids to start a fire, and don't burn garbage.
  • Put smoke detectors in living areas and bedrooms, test them regularly and change their batteries twice a year. A carbon monoxide detector in the same room is highly recommended. Mount detectors in that room as far from the insert as you can, so they don't go off when you add wood.
  • Exhaust fans and clothes dryers can lower the air pressure in the room and make air flow backward through the insert and chimney. Avoid creating that low pressure.
Do not over-fire. If the insert or chimney connector glows, you are over-firing: close the air control immediately. A house fire or serious damage to the insert or chimney could result.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Jøtul's limited warranty (effective January 1, 2019) covers the original retail purchaser from the date of purchase and isn't transferable. Keep your dated sales receipt.

Baffle and air manifold componentsLifetime, parts only
Cast iron and steel components5 years
Enamel finish (peeling, fading)2 years
Blowers, thermostatic switches, combustion monitor1 year
Catalytic combustor (separate warranty)10 years

Not covered

  • Wear and maintenance parts such as paint, gaskets, firebricks, grates and glass (glass only against thermal breakage).
  • Installation or service by anyone other than an authorized installer or service agency, or not done to the instructions and codes.
  • Over-firing (any part glowing red) and misuse. Burning improper materials voids the combustor warranty.

Jøtul must hear about a possible defect within 60 days of when it's found. Contact your Jøtul dealer.

Note: the warranty's section A on p. 28 gives baffle and air manifold components a limited lifetime warranty, parts only; its exclusions on p. 28 list baffles and air manifolds among the normal wear and maintenance parts it doesn't cover.
Note: p. 30 says that if the combustor fails a second time within the 10 years it is covered for 50% off the current retail, and also that any subsequent replacement combustor within the 10-year warranty will be at the current retail price.

specCavity.title: Masonry fireplace requirements
specCavity.html:
Structurally sound, code-approved, solid masonry fireplace only. Not for a factory-built fireplace (p. 9).

A: Front width33" (838 mm)
B: Height23 3/4" (603 mm)
C: Rear width24" (610 mm)
D: Rear height22" (559 mm)

Chimney height15 ft. min · 33 ft. max
  • Front width allows clearance for routing the blower power cord.
  • Clean and inspect the fireplace and chimney to NFPA 211, with a Level II inspection before installation; meet local building code.
  • Repair cracks, broken bricks or flue tiles first. Permanently seal any gap between the hearth extension/fireplace facing and the fire chamber with medium-duty refractory mortar.
  • Don't remove bricks or mortar. Masonry or steel may come out of the smoke shelf and damper frame area for a chimney liner if that doesn't weaken the structure or reduce protection for combustibles.
Note: p. 6 gives the maximum chimney height as 33 ft. and, alongside it, as 10.5 meters; the two figures are not the same length.

specHearth.title: Hearth protection
specHearth.html:
Protect the floor in front of the insert from live sparks and radiant heat with a UL listed Type II hearth board or equivalent mortared masonry (R-value 1.1). Alternates must be noncombustible and meet NFPA 211.

U.S. area16" deep x 37" wide
Canada area20" deep x 37" wide
U.S. front16" from door opening (14 7/8" from surround facing)
Canada front20" from door opening (18 7/8" from surround facing)
Sides, U.S. and Canada18 1/2" each side of centerline

Canada only: front protection may be reduced to 18" when (a) it is noncombustible material with an R-value of 1.1 or higher and (b) it is raised a minimum of 2 1/2" and built on noncombustible materials in a code-approved masonry fireplace.

Checking an alternate material (p. 9)

Convert each layer to R-value (R = 1/k x T, or R = 1/C), add the layers, and accept the alternate if its total R is greater than the specified floor protector's.

specChimney.title: Chimney liner and connection
specChimney.html:
Connect only to a code-approved masonry chimney, with a positive connection to the insert. Never connect to a flue serving another appliance, and don't use aluminum or galvanized steel pipe for chimney connection components.

Chimney sizeNot less than 6", nor more than three times the flue collar's cross-sectional area
U.S.Full stainless steel chimney liner; a 6", 7" or 8" liner, full height, where flue tile is greater than 8" x 12" (damper block-off plate not required, but recommended)
CanadaContinuous 6" (152 mm) liner to the top of the chimney, Class 3 per CAN/ULC-S635 or CAN/ULC-S640

The included Jøtul Draw-Down Adaptor Kit, kit number 156073 (p. 8), makes the liner-to-collar connection; the parts list gives the Draw-Down Flue Collar Adaptor, including pins, as part 222078 (p. 27). The flex liner goes fully into its non-crimped end and is fastened with three sheet metal screws through the pilot holes.

Note: p. 8 says a full stainless steel chimney liner must be installed in the U.S., and p. 9 (Fig. 3.7) says a fully relined chimney is required in the U.S. and Canada; p. 8 also says the 6", 7" or 8" full-height liner is required where the flue tile is greater than 8" x 12", and p. 6 accepts a clay tile liner or a UL 1777 stainless steel liner.

Remove the rear baffle and rear air tube as for flue access, rotate the two front combustor retaining clips 90° and slide them toward the center, then push the catalyst forward from behind the front refractory member, alternating left and right, and lower it out. conflicts.issue: U.S. liner: 'full stainless steel chimney liner must be installed' (p. 8) and Fig. 3.7 'A fully-relined chimney is required in Canada and the U.S.' (p. 9), vs a 6"/7"/8" full-height stainless liner 'required for those installations where the flue tile is greater than 8" x 12"' (p. 8) and 'a clay tile liner or a UL 1777 stainless steel liner' (p. 6).
Maximum chimney height printed as '33 ft. (10.5 meters)'; the metric figure is not the same length as 33 ft.

Section A gives 'baffle and air manifold components' a limited lifetime warranty (parts only), but exclusion 1 lists baffles and air manifolds among normal wear/maintenance parts the warranty does not cover.

Combustor warranty condition 5: a second failure within 10 years 'will be covered for 50 % off the current retail'; condition 8: 'Any subsequent replacement combustor within the 10-year warranty, will be at the current retail price.'

catalog_mismatches.manual: Heating Capacity: Up to 1,700 sq. ft.

review.notes: One combined installation & operation manual (139656_01, 07/25) covering both the Traditional Lattice and Clean Face fronts; the manual never uses the name 'Rockland' (title follows the catalog). Critical dimensions (p. 5, Fig. 2.1) are unlabeled drawing callouts (23 3/4, 21 3/4, 18, 34, 1 1/4 standoff), so overall height/width/depth were not transcribed; the catalog's 30" width can't be checked from the text, and its 23.75 / 18 only match unlabeled callouts. Mantel chart (p. 7, Fig. 3.3) columns A-E are a drawing: only the p. 6 text values (40" at 3 1/2" depth, 46" at 11 1/2") and the 37" heat-shield value the footnote ties to a 3 1/2" mantel and 1" top trim are used. p. 19 reloading text reads 'do load fuel high enough to touch the baffle' (possibly a missing 'not'); left out of the guide. Chimney draft reproduced exactly as printed, '.05 - 1.0 w.c.' (p. 18); worth checking. Minor printed inconsistencies not used in the guide: tools list '5/15" socket bit' vs '5/16" socket' for the pallet screws (p. 4); surround fasteners 'M6 x 10' vs 'M6 x 12' (p. 13); flex conduit kit '1.4" socket driver' (p. 15); CO test method 'CSA B414.1-10' (p. 16) vs 'CSA B415.1-10' (p. 3); pp. 22 and 24 point to 'page 10' for rear-baffle removal, but the steps are on p. 12. p. 24 says combustor removal requires a new insulation wrap (158406) but a note on the same page says a new wrap is required if the removed one has lost integrity; p. 21 says not to overlap the glass gasket rope ends while the general gasket procedure on p. 22 has the tail slightly overlap (neither procedure reproduced in detail). The p. 18 instruction to hold full air until the monitor reads 500°F is placed with the Combustor Thermomonitor text, so it is treated as general operation, not break-in only. No troubleshooting chart or code table: fault panels are built from fault descriptions on pp. 4, 16, 17, 19, 20, 24 and 28; codes left empty. No electrical rating beyond '110vac' (p. 15) and a grounded three-prong plug (p. 20). Catalog 'EPA 2020 certified' is not stated in the manual (only 'EPA - Certified', p. 30). p. 28 says the combustor is secondarily warranted by Performance Industries; p. 30 does not mention it. No French or scrambled text; p. 31 is blank.
